en: The Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya Supāricariyavagga, Chapter 5 I was a king named Kaṇikāra; I possessed a parasol made of kaṇikāra flowers. Having offered that parasol to the Buddha, the Great Sage, I attained the fruit of stream-entry. Through this root of merit, I have been reborn in heaven for eighty-four thousand aeons. In every birth, I have been a king, a lord of the earth, possessing great power and majesty. For eighty-four thousand aeons, I have never experienced even a single unpleasant dream. I have always been handsome, fortunate, and endowed with the marks of a great man. I have always been beloved by many people, and I have enjoyed abundant wealth and grain. I have always been free from illness and disease, and I have always been long-lived. I have always been wise and intelligent, and I have always been skilled in counsel. I have always been a master of the Vedas and the three-fold knowledge, and I have always been a knower of the meaning of the scriptures. I have always been a performer of sacrifices, a giver of offerings, and a protector of the true Dhamma. I have always been a donor of food, drink, clothing, and bedding. I have always given vehicles, lamps, and fragrant incense. I have always given perfumes, garlands, ointments, and various kinds of food. I have always given gold, silver, jewels, pearls, and coral. I have always given elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers. I have always given villages, towns, cities, and entire kingdoms. I have always given wives, children, and my own dear relatives. I have always given my head, hands, feet, eyes, and flesh. I have always given my blood, marrow, and bones. I have always given my heart, liver, and internal organs. I have always given my skin, hair, and nails. I have always given my teeth, tongue, and ears. I have always given my nose, lips, and cheeks. I have always given my forehead, eyebrows, and temples. I have always given my shoulders, arms, and palms. I have always given my back, belly, and flanks. I have always given my thighs, knees, and calves. I have always given my feet, ankles, and toes. I have always given my limbs, joints, and all my members. I have always given my body, life, and everything I possess. I have always given without attachment, and I have always been free from stinginess. I have always given with a joyful heart, and I have always been full of faith. I have always given respectfully, and I have always been humble. I have always given with mindfulness, and I have always been self-controlled. I have always given with wisdom, and I have always been discerning. I have always given with compassion, and I have always been sympathetic. I have always given with kindness, and I have always been benevolent. I have always given with a mind of loving-kindness, and I have always been peaceful. I have always given with equanimity, and I have always been impartial. I have always given without discrimination, and I have always been consistent. I have always given at all times, and I have always been constant. I have always given in all places, and I have always been universal. I have always given to all beings, and I have always been inclusive. I have always given to the poor, the destitute, and the suffering. I have always given to the sick, the aged, and the helpless. I have always given to the virtuous, the learned, and the noble. I have always given to the monks, the nuns, and the lay followers. I have always given to the Buddhas, the Pacceka Buddhas, and the Arahants. I have always given to the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the Triple Gem. Through this root of merit, I have attained the state of an Arahant. I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, and I have reached the further shore. I have extinguished the fires of craving, and I have attained Nibbāna. This is the Apadāna of the Elder Kaṇikārachattiya, in the Supāricariyavagga, the fifth chapter.
“The Fully Enlightened One named Vessabhū,
the eldest in the world, the bull among men—
the Sage— for his midday rest, [entered the village of Bandhumatī.]”
I entered the great forest.
Having plucked a kaṇikāra flower,
I then made it into a parasol.
Having fashioned a floral canopy,
I offered it to the Buddha.
Thirty-one eons ago from now,
The flower that I offered— of this worship of the Buddha,
I do not know a state of woe;
this is the fruit thereof.
In this twentieth aeon,
there were eight Kṣatriyas named Soṇṇābha,
who were endowed with the seven treasures.
Universal monarchs of great power.
The four analytical knowledges... [and so forth]...
“Thus was the teaching of the Buddha spoken.
Thus indeed did the venerable elder Kaṇikārachattiya speak these verses.
This is the fifth legend of the elder Kaṇikārachattiya.
